L19: # Authentication overview
L20: 
L21: Learn how to manage authentication for your apps and when developing locally.
L22: 
L23: While building apps on the developer platform, you can configure authentication based on how you plan to install your app. HubSpot also provides local authentication tooling via the HubSpot CLI.
L24: ##
L25: 
L26: cite3†​ L27: 
L28: App authentication
L29: 
L30: There are two authentication types available based on how you plan to distribute your app: OAuth is required for multiple accounts, while static auth access tokens are used for installing in a single account at a time.
L31: ###
L32: 
L33: cite4†​ L34: 
L35: OAuth
L36: If you plan to distribute your app to multiple accounts (either through listing on the HubSpot Marketplace or by managing specific authorized accounts), your app must be built using OAuth authentication. You’ll need to set up and host an OAuth backend service (e.g., hosted as a Docker instance using a cloud service provider) to initiate the OAuth process and manage token data for users installing your app in their account.
L37: HubSpot provides a Node.js quickstart guide cite5†here , which includes code you can run in a Docker instance with full OAuth support. Authentication configuration details for your app are available on the app details page in the cite6†developer overview of your HubSpot account. Once you’ve set up an OAuth backend, you can make API requests using the OAuth access token that corresponds to a user who installed your app. This access token is provided using the `Bearer` HTTP authorization header.
L38: For example, if you wanted to retrieve contacts for the account with an access token of `00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz`, your request would resemble the following:
L39: 
L40:     `curl --request GET \
L41:     --header "Authorization: Bearer 00000000-aaaa-xxx-yyyy-zzzzzzzzzzzz" \
L42:     --url "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/objects/2026-03/contacts?limit=10&archived=false"
L43:     `
L44: Configure your app to use OAuth by setting the `type` subproperty within the `auth` field of your app’s `app-hsmeta.json` config to `oauth`. You’ll also need to set the `distribution` property to `marketplace` or `private` based on how you plan to distribute your app:
L45:   * `marketplace`: used if you want the app to be eligible for listing on the HubSpot Marketplace.
L46:   * `private`: used if you only want to install your app in a specific set of allowlisted accounts. If you choose this option, you can install your app in a maximum of 10 accounts at a time.
L47: Learn more in the cite7†app configuration guide .
L48: ###
L49: 
L50: cite8†​ L51: 
L52: Static auth
L53: 
L54: If you want to limit distribution of your app to a single authorized account, you’ll use a static auth access token. This token can be found in your cite6†app settings . An example request is provided below using a placeholder static auth access token.
L55: 
L56:     `curl --request GET \
L57:     --header "Authorization: Bearer ***-***-*********-****-****-****-************" \
L58:     --url "https://api.hubapi.com/crm/objects/2026-03/contacts?limit=10&archived=false"
L59:     `
L60: Configure your app to use static auth by setting the `type` subproperty (within the `auth` field) in your app’s `app-hsmeta.json` config to `static`, and set the `distribution` field to `private`. Learn more in the cite7†app configuration guide .
L61: ##
L62: 
L63: cite9†​ L64: 
L65: Developer API keys
L66: Some app features and settings require a developer API key, which is available in the developer overview of your HubSpot account. If a feature or endpoint requires a developer API key, it’ll be documented in the associated guide or reference article. You’ll provide the key value in the `hapikey` query parameter, usually with the `appId` query parameter which corresponds to the app you’re making changes to.
L67: For example, the `cURL` snippet below provides an example of using the cite10†custom channel registration endpoint:
L68: 
L69:     `curl --request POST \
L70:     --url "https://api.hubapi.com/conversations/custom-channels/2026-03?hapikey={YOUR_DEVELOPER_API_KEY}&appId={appId}"
L71:     `
L72: ##
L73: 
L74: cite11†​ L75: 
L76: Client credentials
L77: Similar to HubSpot developer API keys, HubSpot uses client credential tokens to take an action on behalf of your app. These tokens are OAuth 2.0 tokens with short-term expiry windows that must be refreshed after a certain amount of time. Unlike the OAuth tokens used for app authentication, client credential tokens aren’t used to act on behalf of users who install your app. Instead, they’re used to manage your app’s global configuration for specific features.
L78: Currently, the only feature using client credential tokens is the cite12†webhooks journal API . For example, to generate a client credentials token with all available webhook journal and management permissions, you’d make the following API call:
L79: 
L80:     `curl --location 'https://api.hubapi.com/oauth/2026-03/token' \
L81:       --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
L82:       --data-urlencode 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
L83:       --data-urlencode 'client_id=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX' \
L84:       --data-urlencode 'client_secret=XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX' \
L85:       --data-urlencode 'scope=developer.webhooks_journal.read developer.webhooks_journal.subscriptions.read developer.webhooks_journal.subscriptions.write developer.webhooks_journal.snapshots.read developer.webhooks_journal.snapshots.write'
L86:     `
L87: ##
L88: 
L89: cite13†​ L90: 
L91: Scopes
L92: 
L93: Based on the HubSpot data and functionality that your app will require access to, you’ll provide a list of scopes in your app’s `app-hsmeta.json` authentication config. For example, if your app required access to create contacts, you’d need to include the `crm.objects.contacts.write`. Learn more about cite14†scopes .
L94: ##
L95: 
L96: cite15†​ L97: 
L98: Local authentication
L99: 
L100: While you develop your app locally using the HubSpot CLI, you can use the `hs accounts auth` command. If you’re configuring local authentication for the first time, you can also use the `hs init` command. After authenticating, a cite16†personal access key will be associated with your account that will be used to authenticate CLI commands. Learn more about cite17†installing the HubSpot CLI . A full list of CLI commands is provided cite18†here .
L101: ##
L102: 
L103: cite19†​ L104: 
L105: Client secret rotation
L106: A client secret is a confidential value specific to your app, which is used for managing cite20†OAuth tokens , validating cite21†requests from HubSpot , and generating a cite11†client credentials token . If this secret is compromised (e.g., you mistakenly committed the secret to a git repository), you can rotate the secret to ensure the old one is invalidated and cannot be used.
L107: Client secret rotation is supported for cite22†legacy public apps , project-based apps on the cite23†developer platform , and cite24†MCP auth apps . Learn how to rotate a cite25†client secret in a project-based app.

L17: # Quickstart
L18: 
L19: Build with Clay from your coding agent, or call the Clay API from your own applications.
L20: 
L21: There are two ways to use Clay as a developer: install the agent plugin to build with Clay inside your coding agent, or call the Public API directly from your own applications and services.
L22: ##
L23: 
L24: cite3†​ L25: 
L26: Agent plugin
L27: The agent plugin gives your coding agent Clay’s skills and the `clay` CLI — the fastest way to build with Clay from a coding agent. It requires a coding-agent host with a shell — Claude Code, Codex, or Cursor — and doesn’t work in general-purpose chat apps like Claude Desktop, claude.ai, or ChatGPT that can’t run the CLI. Copy this into your agent of choice and let it install and set up the plugin for you:
L28: 
L29:     `Set up the Clay plugin by following the steps in
L30:     https://github.com/clay-run/agent-plugins
L31:     `
L32: This runs the plugin’s `setup` skill, which puts `clay` on your PATH, signs you in, and verifies the CLI. Sign-in opens a browser to authorize the CLI.
L33: ## Agent plugin repository
L34: 
L35: Manual install and setup instructions for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.
L36: 
L37: ##
L38: 
L39: cite4†​ L40: 
L41: API
L42: 
L43: Use the Public API to call Clay from your own applications and services — backend jobs, internal tools, queues, and product features. Requests authenticate with a Clay API key in the `clay-api-key` header.
L44: 
L45: ## API reference
L46: 
L47: Endpoint paths, request bodies, response schemas, and an interactive try-it console.
L48: ###
L49: 
L50: cite5†​ L51: 
L52: Get an API key
L53: 
L54: You can create an API key two ways:
L55: 
L56:   * Ask your agent to generate one for you after installing the cite3†agent plugin .
L57:   * Create one yourself in Clay under cite6†Settings → Account → API keys (beta)†app.clay.com .
L58: Keep keys server-side. Do not expose them in browser code, mobile apps, public repositories, logs, or analytics tools. See cite7†Authentication for details.
L59:

L660: # API Accounts
L661: 
L662: BigCommerce offers a suite of APIs that let you manage store data, sign customers in, make client-side queries for product information, and write apps that integrate third-party services into store operations.
L663: BigCommerce API accounts play a role in every authenticated request to our servers. Our API accounts come in a few different flavors to meet the needs of different use cases. For example, app API accounts work well in multi-store contexts, whereas store API accounts are a good choice for frontend applications. Some endpoints only work with one kind of API account.
L664: 
L665: For an overview of the authentication schemes that our APIs use, see the cite595†Authentication section below.
L666: ## API accounts
L667: 
L668: BigCommerce offers three types of OAuth-based API accounts to developers who wish to use BigCommerce’s REST APIs: store-level credentials, app-level credentials, and account-level credentials. This section describes the difference between the three, how to obtain and revoke account credentials, and the use cases for each. It also contains a reference for available OAuth scopes and provides a compelling list of reasons to migrate from legacy API tokens to OAuth credentials.
L669: Every parent set of API credentials that you request for your store is its own API account. At its simplest, an API account consists of the following:
L670: 
L671:   * The `client_id` uniquely identifies the app or user, or the client, making a request.
L672:   * The `client_secret` is a cryptographically secure value known only to the client and BigCommerce.
L673: Every active API account has at least one `access_token`. cite573†Store-level API accounts include a static access token that does not change. cite579†App-level API accounts expect each application to generate a unique access token for every store that installs the app. cite584†Account-level API accounts include a single access token that belongs to the parent account of the store that the user is signed in to at the time of creation.
L674: Guard these values closely. The client ID and client secret will never change; access tokens do not expire based on time and cannot be manually invalidated. It’s best practice to limit each account’s cite591†OAuth scope to only the privileges needed to complete that app or user’s designated tasks. Create separate API accounts for each app, store API user or function, or account-related implementation.
L675: ### Choosing the right kind of API account
L676: 
L677: Where both types of API account are supported, review the preceding sections to make an informed choice about which best fits your use case.
L678: API or Use Case  | Store-level API account  | App-level API account  | Account-level API account
L679: --- | --- | --- | ---
L680: cite597†GraphQL Account API , including cite614†Users |  |  | ×
L681: cite597†GraphQL Admin API | ×  | ×  |
L682: cite604†GraphQL Storefront API | ×  |  |
L683: cite597†B2B REST Management API | ×  |  |
L684: cite597†REST Store Management APIs | ×  | ×  |
L685: cite609†REST Storefront API | ×  |  |
L686: cite606†Customer Login API |  | ×  |
L687: cite600†Current Customer API |  | ×  |
L688: cite604†Payments API | ×  | ×  |
L689: cite611†Apps that host REST Provider APIs (provider apps) |  | ×  |
L690: cite615†Apps that create App Extensions |  | ×  |
L691: Apps hosted in the store control panel (single-click apps)  |  | ×  |
L692: Manual connection between a third-party app and a store  | ×  |  | ×
L693: Single-store frontend scripts  |  | ×  |
L694: ### Store-level API accounts
L695: 
L696: Merchants generate single-store API credentials when they create API accounts in their store control panel, in the cite616†Settings > Store-level API accounts†login.bigcommerce.com menu. Use these credentials to read and change one store’s data with BigCommerce’s APIs. You can’t change store-level access tokens or OAuth scopes.
L697: 
L698: In addition to the cite571†API account components in the preceding section, store-level API accounts contain the following attributes out of the box:
L699:   * An `access_token`, which accompanies most REST API requests.
L700:   * The client name is a label for your convenience, and it doesn’t accompany requests.
L701:   * The API path is the URL to which you make requests. The API path won’t change, but it will have `/v3/` or `/v2/` appended to it, depending on the current version for the endpoint you’re querying.
L702: Most APIs that work with store-level API accounts use the `access_token` to authenticate requests to BigCommerce. However, a few use the access token to generate a temporary credential. To learn more about special cases that involve store-level credentials, consult the documentation for the API you want to use.
L703: #### Be careful with client secrets
L704: 
L705: Do not send your `client_secret` or `access_token` in plain text or an unencrypted payload. Be particularly careful with the `client_secret`. An attacker can use your `client_secret` to both sign and decrypt JWTs sent between you and BigCommerce.
L706: 
L707: #### Creating store-level API credentials
L708: 
L709: To create a store-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on cite617†Creating a Store API Account†support.bigcommerce.com .
L710: #### Revoking store-level API credentials
L711: 
L712: To revoke store-level API credentials, you must delete the corresponding store API account. If the `client_id` and `client_secret` are compromised, or the account has become unnecessary, secure your account by deleting the API account. You cannot recover a deleted API account, so take care.
L713: #### Delete carefully
L714: 
L715: Deleting an account cannot be undone, so be sure before clicking the trash can icon. You can also use the checkboxes on the left side to delete multiple accounts at once – but be especially careful when using this option.
L716: 
L717: To delete a store-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on cite618†Deleting a Store API Account†support.bigcommerce.com .
L718: #### Don’t forget your webhooks and metafields
L719: 
L720: Some resources are only accessible to the API account that created them. These include webhooks, metafields, and scripts. If you need to revoke a store-level API account, plan accordingly.
L721: 
L722: Webhooks do not persist upon account deletion. Verify webhooks associated with an account before deleting it.
L723: ### App-level API accounts
L724: 
L725: You can cite580†create app-level API accounts in the cite619†Developer Portal†build.bigcommerce.com . After a store owner or authorized user installs and authorizes an app, most apps use access tokens generated from the API account’s client ID, client secret, and a temporary grant code to read and change store data. cite581†Generate access tokens with the BigCommerce-initiated grant code authorization flow.
L726: Some APIs use app-level API accounts to implement alternative authentication patterns. For a summary of all our authentication methods, see the cite596†authentication schemes described earlier in this article.
L727: 
L728: For more on working with apps, see our cite348†Guide to Building Apps . The sections on cite357†Implementing OAuth and cite358†Callback Handlers are particularly relevant to generating access tokens.
L729: #### Creating app-level API credentials
L730: 
L731: To create an app and its associated API account, consult our article on cite620†Managing Apps in the Developer Portal .
L732: 
L733: #### App-level access tokens
L734: 
L735: App-level API accounts do not come pre-configured with an access token. Each time a store installs your app, BigCommerce initiates a grant code authorization flow to help your app generate a dedicated access token for that store. For further details, see cite357†Authenticating an app .
L736: #### Revoking app-level API credentials
L737: 
L738: There is no way to manually revoke or force-regenerate app-level API account access tokens. However, either of the following actions triggers a token refresh:
L739: 
L740:   * When the store owner’s email address changes
L741:   * When you modify the app API account’s OAuth scopes
L742: 
L743: After one of these changes, the store owner will be prompted to review the change and reauthorize the app the next time they click the app icon in the store control panel.
L744: #### Delete apps carefully
L745: 
L746: When you delete an app in the cite619†Dev Portal†build.bigcommerce.com , there is no way to recover the client ID or client secret. If you choose to do this, don’t forget to mitigate the potential loss of cite578†webhook and metafield -related data and functionality.
L747: 
L748: To delete an app-level API account, consult our article on cite621†Managing Apps in the Developer Portal .
L749: ### Account-level API accounts
L750: Account-level API accounts are designed to work with the GraphQL Account API, which manages resources beyond the scope of a single store. For example, cite614†managing control panel users in the BigCommerce ecosystem. Current and future features available using the GraphQL Account API toolset allow developers to build custom integrations and solutions that require high-level access to store and platform resources.
L751: Using this API, you can integrate with third-party applications, streamline and automate business processes, and manage multiple merchant stores per account.
L752: #### Creating account-level credentials
L753: 
L754: To create an account-level API account visit the cite622†account control panel†accounts.bigcommerce.com or the store control panel for a member store at cite616†Settings > Account-level API accounts†login.bigcommerce.com .
L755: 
L756: To learn more about creating an account-level API account, consult our Knowledge Base article on cite623†API Accounts†support.bigcommerce.com .
L757: When you create account-level credentials, they belong to the parent account for the store you’re signed in to.
L758: 
L759: Account-level API credentials provide direct access to all the account’s stores, not just the store that was signed in at the time of creation. Their permissions are limited only by the OAuth scopes they were granted at the time of creation. Keep the access token and client secret secure.
L760: #### Revoking account-level API credentials
L761: 
L762: An account-level access token is valid until the account is no longer active. However, you can manually delete account-level credentials.
L763: 
L764: Deleting API accounts is risky and must be done with caution. Only users who have the correct permissions can perform this action.
L765: To delete an account-level API account, visit the cite622†account control panel†accounts.bigcommerce.com and find the account you want to delete in the list. Click the three dots in the Action column, then click Delete. Follow any prompts that appear.
L766: ### Migrating from legacy to OAuth
L767: 
L768: #### Legacy API Accounts
L769: 
L770: BigCommerce no longer issues legacy API Accounts to new stores. Existing legacy API Accounts will continue to work until further notice. Migrate to OAuth as soon as possible.
L771: #### Benefits of migrating to OAuth
L772: 
L773: We recommend migrating from legacy API credentials to OAuth, if you haven’t already. Migration provides a wealth of benefits, including the following:
L774: 
L775:   * Unified requests: Send all OAuth requests to a single URL: `https://api.bigcommerce.com`. Using a common hostname prevents interruptions of service when a store’s domain or SSL/TLS certificate changes or expires.
L776: 
L777:   * Latest and greatest APIs: BigCommerce’s V3 APIs are accessible exclusively with OAuth.
L778:   * Webhook subscriptions: OAuth API accounts can subscribe to real-time event notifications using BigCommerce’s webhooks.
L779: 
L780:   * Shared secrets: Use new APIs and endpoints that require shared secrets, including the cite172†Customer Login and cite173†Current Customer APIs.
L781: 
L782:   * Zippier responses: Responses to OAuth requests use gzip compression and less of your bandwidth.
L783:   * Better security with granular permissions: All OAuth tokens are scoped to specific operations and endpoints. If you suspect a breach, you will know which resources could be affected.
L784: #### How to migrate
L785: 
L786: Before you update your API connections to use OAuth instead of legacy basic authentication, take the following actions:
L787:   * Create an API account appropriate to your use case. Keeping in mind the API endpoints your connections use, create either a store API account or an app API account per the preceding instructions. To adhere to industry-standard security practices, configure the account with the minimum OAuth scopes for your use case. If you’re using an app API account, you can always modify the scope later.
L788:   * If you use one of our cite6†client libraries , consult the library’s documentation for establishing an optimal OAuth configuration.
L789:   * After you create your connection, update your connection parameters as follows:
L790:     * Use `https://api.bigcommerce.com` as the gateway URL instead of the BigCommerce store’s secure hostname. For example, route requests that formerly went to `https://store-{{store_hash}}.mybigcommerce.com/api/v2/orders/{{order_id}}` or `https://my-custom-store-domain.com/api/v2/orders/{{order_id}}` will now use `https://api.bigcommerce.com/stores/{{store_hash}}/v2/orders/{{order_id}}`.
L791:     * Rewrite your HTTP request headers to use the `X-Auth-Token` header to pass the API account’s `access_token` instead of the `Authorization` header. For more information, see the cite597†access tokens section above.
L792: Rate limiting works differently for OAuth API connections. For details, see the cite9†Rate Limits section of our API best practices article.
L793: ## OAuth scopes
L794: 
L795: Scope grants and limits a program’s ability to read and write data. Set the scopes to the minimum level of access your implementation needs.
L796: 
L797: All OAuth scopes except `default` provide `read-only` permissions scopes so that you can limit some accounts to sending `GET` and `HEAD` requests.
L798: 
L799: Webhooks are accessible from the default scope that is automatically accessible to all API accounts.
